chapters.title: The rules of interaction

chapters.goals: Discover the QED vertex and charge conservation. Tell what is allowed from what can actually happen.

chapters.title: Interacting particles
chapters.subtitle: Exchanges and virtual lines
chapters.goals: Combine two vertices, build exchanges and tell internal lines from external ones.

levels.title: Your first diagram
levels.intro: Richard Feynman invented a visual language to describe how particles interact. Each line is a particle, and time runs from left to right. Let's learn its first letters.

steps.prompt: Straight lines with an arrow represent electrons. Tap one.

wrong.int: That line is wavy: it's a photon. Look for a straight one with an arrow.

steps.wrongDefault: Look for a straight line with an arrow in the middle.
hints: There are four straight lines: two on the left and two on the right.
Any straight line with an arrow will do: they're all electrons.
steps.solved: That's it! Straight with an arrow: electron (e⁻).

steps.prompt: The wavy line is a photon, the particle of light. Tap it.
steps.wrongDefault: That line is straight: it's an electron. The photon is drawn wavy.
hints: Look for the only line that isn't straight.
It's in the middle, joining the two points where the lines meet.

steps.prompt: With the convention we use, which way does time run in the diagram?

options.feedback: On the left, what comes in; on the right, what goes out.
Some books use that convention, but here time always flows from left to right (look at the axis at the bottom).
They do have a time direction: it separates the initial state (left) from the final one (right).

hints: Look at the arrow below the diagram.
The initial particles are drawn on the left.

levels.success: You can read your first two “letters”! Straight with an arrow: electron. Wavy: photon.

explanation.intuitive: Two electrons approach, exchange a photon and move apart. That's how two negative charges repel each other.
explanation.scientific: It's a tree-level electron–electron scattering diagram (Møller scattering). The four external fermion lines are the initial and final electrons; the internal wavy line is a virtual photon.
explanation.math: Each element of the diagram contributes a factor to a probability amplitude 𝓜. This diagram has two vertices, so its contribution is proportional to e², where e is the elementary charge.

levels.title: In and out
levels.intro: Every diagram tells a story: some particles come in (initial state) and others go out (final state). In between, they interact.

steps.prompt: Tap all the particles of the initial state (the ones coming in) and press Check.

wrong.int: That photon is internal: it starts and ends inside the diagram, so it neither comes in nor goes out.

steps.wrongDefault: That line reaches the right edge: it leaves the process.
hints: The particles coming in are on the left.
They're the two straight lines touching the left edge.

steps.prompt: How many particles are there in the final state?

options.feedback: Two electrons leave on the right.
The photon doesn't count: it joins two vertices inside the diagram, so it doesn't go out.
Count only the lines that reach the right edge.

hints: Count the lines that reach the right edge.
The central photon doesn't reach any edge.

steps.prompt: Two electrons come in and two electrons go out. What role does the photon play?

options.text: It carries the electromagnetic interaction between them
options.feedback: The photon is the mediator of the electromagnetic force.

options.text: It's a third electron being created
options.feedback: It's wavy: it's a photon, not an electron.

options.text: It escapes and we could detect it
options.feedback: A photon joining two vertices is internal (virtual): it never reaches a detector.

hints: The photon joins the two points where something happens.
Think of it as the force's “messenger”.

levels.success: You can now tell the beginning from the end of a quantum story.

explanation.intuitive: What comes in is on the left; what goes out, on the right. The central photon is the “messenger” of the interaction.
explanation.scientific: External lines represent real particles of the initial and final states, the ones prepared and detected in an experiment. Internal lines represent virtual particles, which aren't observed directly.
explanation.math: For each initial and final state we compute an amplitude 𝓜. The probability of the process is proportional to |𝓜|².

levels.title: The backward arrow
levels.intro: Every particle has an antiparticle with the opposite charge. The electron's is the positron (e⁺). It's drawn with the same straight line, but with the arrow pointing against time.

steps.prompt: Tap the positron coming into the interaction.

wrong.in1: That one comes in, but its arrow points forward in time: it's an electron.
wrong.out2: It's a positron, but it's on the right: it goes out. Look for the one coming in.
wrong.out1: That line goes out and its arrow points forward in time: it's an electron.

steps.wrongDefault: Look for a line on the left with the arrow pointing left.
hints: Look only at the lines on the left.
The positron's arrow points backward in time, that is, to the left.

steps.prompt: What electric charge does a positron have?

options.feedback: Same mass as the electron, opposite charge.
An antiparticle has the opposite charge to its particle.
The positron has charge: that's why it can emit and absorb photons.

hints: “Anti” means opposite.
The electron's charge is −1.

steps.prompt: Now tap the positron going out.

wrong.out1: It goes out, but with the arrow forward in time: it's an electron.

steps.wrongDefault: Look on the right for an arrow pointing left.
hints: It's on the right.
Its arrow also points left, against time.

levels.success: You've discovered antimatter. The same line, with the arrow reversed.

explanation.intuitive: An electron and a positron pass each other and are deflected by exchanging a photon.
explanation.scientific: It's Bhabha scattering (e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺) in the t channel. The arrow doesn't show where the particle moves, but the flow of fermion number. An arrow against time represents an antiparticle moving into the future.
explanation.math: In the amplitude, an incoming electron contributes a spinor u(p) and an incoming positron a spinor v̄(p). The order is still e².

levels.title: Name every line
levels.intro: You now know the electron, the positron and the photon. With these three pieces you can write all of quantum electrodynamics (QED). Read this new diagram.

steps.prompt: Tap all the photons in the diagram and press Check.

wrong.int: That line is straight: it's a (virtual) electron, even though it's inside the diagram.
wrong.in2: Straight with the arrow pointing backward: it's a positron.
wrong.in1: Straight with the arrow pointing forward: it's an electron.

hints: There's more than one photon.
Both photons are on the right.

steps.prompt: What process does this diagram represent?

options.text: An electron and a positron annihilate and produce two photons
options.feedback: Matter and antimatter turn into light.

options.text: Two photons collide and create an electron and a positron
options.feedback: Look at the direction of time: the photons are on the right, so they go out.

options.text: An electron emits two photons and carries on
options.feedback: The bottom line has its arrow pointing backward: it's a positron, not another electron.

hints: What comes in on the left?
One arrow forward and one backward: an electron and a positron.

levels.success: You're reading diagrams you'd never seen before. That's how you learn a language.

explanation.intuitive: When an electron meets a positron, they can disappear and turn into light: two photons.
explanation.scientific: It's the annihilation of an electron–positron pair into two photons (e⁻e⁺ → γγ). The internal line is a virtual electron joining the two vertices. It's used, for example, in positron emission tomography (PET).
explanation.math: Again there are two vertices, so the amplitude is of order e². There's another diagram with the photons swapped, and it's added to this one to get the total amplitude.

levels.title: Not a photograph
levels.intro: Feynman's language is very precise: a wrong label changes the meaning. This diagram has a notation mistake. Can you find it?

steps.prompt: One label doesn't match what the drawing says. Tap the mislabelled line.
steps.wrongDefault: That line's label matches its drawing. Check which way each arrow points.
hints: Compare each arrow with the direction of time.
A line with the arrow pointing backward should be called e⁺.
steps.solved: Backward arrow coming in: it's a positron, not an electron.

steps.prompt: A friend says: “The top electron travels exactly along that path and bounces off the photon.” What would you tell her?

options.text: The diagram isn't a trajectory: it represents a contribution to the probability of the process
options.feedback: Exactly. The positions and angles in the drawing mean nothing: all that matters is what's connected to what.

options.text: She's right: the lines are the real paths
options.feedback: Quantum particles don't follow definite paths like balls. If we draw the diagram differently, it means the same thing.

options.text: Almost: the real path is curved
options.feedback: Neither straight nor curved: the diagram doesn't describe any path in space.

hints: Would the physics change if we drew the lines longer or tilted?
A Feynman diagram is a piece of a calculation of probability amplitudes.

levels.success: You found the mistake and avoided the most common misconception about Feynman diagrams.

explanation.intuitive: A Feynman diagram is like a subway map: it tells you what's connected to what, not exactly where things go.
explanation.scientific: A Feynman diagram represents a contribution to the probability amplitude of a process. It's not a photograph of trajectories: the positions of vertices and lines on paper have no physical meaning, only the topology and the line types.
explanation.math: Each vertex of the diagram is integrated over every position in spacetime. That's why the drawing doesn't fix any particular trajectory.

levels.title: The meeting point
levels.intro: Lines don't just cross: they meet at points called vertices. There, and only there, the interaction happens. This is an isolated vertex: the basic piece of every diagram.

steps.prompt: Tap the vertex in the diagram.
steps.wrongDefault: That point is an endpoint: a particle coming in or going out. The vertex is where the lines join.
hints: Look for the point where several lines come together.
It's the bright point in the middle.
steps.solved: That's the vertex: the place where the interaction happens.

steps.prompt: How many lines meet at this vertex?

options.feedback: Count the wavy line too.
Three lines: always three in QED.
Count again the lines reaching the central point.

hints: Count the lines touching the central point.
There are two straight ones and one wavy one.

steps.prompt: Which combination of lines forms a QED vertex?

options.text: Two fermion lines (one arrow in and one out) and a photon
options.feedback: This is QED's only interaction rule.
Photons have no charge: they don't interact directly with each other in QED.
Charge wouldn't be conserved, and in QED the interaction always goes through a photon.

hints: Look at which kinds of line touch the vertex.
One of the arrows arrives at the vertex and the other leaves it.

levels.success: You've discovered QED's fundamental rule: one vertex, three lines.

explanation.intuitive: An electron can emit or absorb a photon. All of electricity, magnetism and light comes from this single rule.
explanation.scientific: The QED vertex couples the electron field to the photon field. It always joins one incoming fermion line, one outgoing fermion line and one photon line. The same vertex, rotated, describes emission, absorption, annihilation or pair creation.
explanation.math: Each vertex contributes a factor −ieγ^μ, where e is the elementary charge and γ^μ are the Dirac matrices.

levels.title: The arrow doesn't break
levels.intro: Now it's your turn to build. At each vertex, the arrow that comes in must carry on going out. That's how charge conservation is drawn.

steps.prompt: Complete the vertex: the electron must leave on the right. Drag from the vertex to the exit point.
hints: The arrow follows the direction of your gesture.
An outgoing electron has its arrow pointing right: drag from the vertex outward.
steps.solved: The arrow comes in and goes out: charge is conserved.

steps.prompt: A positron comes in at the bottom and meets an electron. Draw the positron's line with the correct arrow.
hints: An incoming positron has its arrow pointing against time.
Drag from the vertex to the entry point at the bottom: that way the arrow points left.

levels.success: You've drawn charge conservation with a simple arrow.

explanation.intuitive: What comes in on one side goes out on the other: the arrow is never cut or duplicated.
explanation.scientific: Arrows form continuous lines that pass through the vertices. This expresses conservation of fermion number and, in QED, of electric charge. An incoming electron (−1) and an incoming positron (+1) add up to 0, the photon's charge.
explanation.math: Charge conservation follows from QED's U(1) gauge symmetry (Noether's theorem). At each vertex, the current ψ̄γ^μψ is conserved.

levels.title: Impossible vertices
levels.intro: A lab engineer has drawn some diagrams with mistakes. Use the rules you know to find what's wrong.

steps.prompt: This vertex connects two electrons and two photons. What's wrong with it as a fundamental vertex?

options.text: A QED vertex joins exactly three lines: two fermion lines and a photon
options.feedback: There is no fundamental four-line vertex in QED.

options.text: Nothing: a vertex can have as many photons as it likes
options.feedback: QED has only one kind of vertex, with exactly one photon.
They can: that's exactly what a correct three-line vertex describes.

hints: Count the lines at the vertex.
The rule from level 6: three lines, one of them a photon.
steps.solved: That process exists, but it's drawn with two chained vertices, not with one four-line vertex.

steps.prompt: In this diagram one vertex violates charge conservation. Tap the culprit line and flip its arrow.
hints: Check the arrows vertex by vertex: at each one, one must come in and another go out.
Two arrows come into the top vertex. The editable line is the top exit.

levels.success: You spot vertices that nature doesn't allow. You're the lab's quality control.

explanation.intuitive: QED has only one interaction rule. If a drawing breaks it, it doesn't describe anything that can happen.
explanation.scientific: The QED Lagrangian contains only one interaction term, ψ̄γ^μψA_μ, with two fermion fields and one photon. That's why there's a single fundamental three-line vertex. Processes like e⁻γ → e⁻γ (Compton) are described by chaining two vertices.
explanation.math: A term with two photons and two electrons would have mass dimension 5 and make the theory non-renormalizable. It doesn't appear in QED.

levels.title: Allowed isn't possible
levels.intro: A correct vertex is a valid piece of the language. But can it happen on its own in nature? Here physics sets you a little trap.

steps.prompt: This vertex follows the rules of QED. Can a free, isolated electron emit a real photon like this, with nothing else?

options.text: No: it can't conserve both energy and momentum
options.feedback: In the rest frame of the initial electron, there's no energy available to create a photon.

options.text: Yes: electrons emit light all the time
options.feedback: Electrons emit light when they interact with something (a nucleus, a field, another electron). A lone electron in vacuum can't.

hints: Imagine the electron at rest before emitting.
Where would the photon's energy come from if the electron can't lose mass?

steps.prompt: And a lone photon in vacuum? Can it turn into an electron and a positron?

options.text: Not on its own: it needs another particle nearby, such as a nucleus, to absorb momentum
options.feedback: That's why pair creation is seen when a high-energy photon passes close to a nucleus.

options.text: Yes, if it has enough energy
options.feedback: Not even with all the energy in the world. In the frame where the pair has zero total momentum, the photon would need zero momentum and non-zero energy, which is impossible for a photon.

hints: A photon always moves at the speed of light and always has momentum.
The e⁻e⁺ pair can be at rest as a whole; the photon never can.

steps.prompt: So what's an isolated vertex good for?

options.text: It's a piece: real processes are built by combining vertices
options.feedback: With two or more vertices, the internal lines can be virtual and the process can happen.

options.text: Nothing: it's a flaw in the formalism
options.feedback: It's the piece everything else is built from.

hints: Think of letters and words.
In the next chapter you'll combine two vertices.

levels.success: You've learned a subtlety that confuses many students: allowed doesn't mean possible.

explanation.intuitive: The drawing rules say which pieces exist. Conservation laws say which complete processes can really happen.
explanation.scientific: A formally allowed diagram doesn't guarantee that the process can happen with real external particles. Three-particle processes with free particles in QED (e → eγ, γ → e⁺e⁻, e⁺e⁻ → γ) violate conservation of four-momentum. Inside bigger diagrams, virtual internal lines get around this restriction.
explanation.math: For e(p) → e(p′) + γ(k): (p − k)² = m² implies m² − 2p·k = m², that is, p·k = 0. But for a massive electron and a real photon with positive energy, p·k > 0. Contradiction.

levels.title: Design your vertex
levels.intro: The same vertex, rotated, describes different processes. Build two versions from scratch, as pieces of bigger diagrams.

steps.prompt: Build the vertex where a photon turns into an electron (top) and a positron (bottom).
hints: The photon first: pick the wavy line and join it to the vertex.
Outgoing electron: from the vertex outward. Outgoing positron: from outside toward the vertex.
steps.solved: Pair creation: a continuous arrow that “turns around” at the vertex.

steps.prompt: Now a positron that emits a photon and carries on.
hints: The positron comes in and goes out: both arrows point against time.
Drag from the exit to the vertex and from the vertex to the entry.

levels.success: You've discovered crossing symmetry: a single vertex, many stories.

explanation.intuitive: Rotate the vertex and what was an emission becomes a pair creation. It's the same rule seen from another angle.
explanation.scientific: Crossing symmetry relates processes in which an incoming particle is replaced by its outgoing antiparticle. Emission, absorption, annihilation and pair creation are the same vertex with different orientations with respect to time.
explanation.math: The amplitudes of crossed processes are obtained by analytic continuation, changing p → −p for the crossed particle.

levels.title: Inside and outside
levels.intro: With two vertices something new appears: lines that neither come in nor go out, but join one vertex to another. They're internal lines.

steps.prompt: Tap all the internal lines (the ones joining two vertices) and press Check.
steps.wrongDefault: That line reaches an edge of the diagram: it's external.
hints: An internal line doesn't touch any edge.
There's only one, and it's wavy.

steps.prompt: Now select all the external lines and press Check.

wrong.int: That photon joins two vertices: it's internal.

hints: External lines touch the left or the right edge.
There are four.

steps.prompt: How many vertices does this diagram have?

options.feedback: Two vertices joined by an internal line.
The ends of the external lines aren't vertices: no interaction happens there.

hints: A vertex is where three lines join.
The endpoints on the edges don't count.

levels.success: External: what is observed. Internal: what happens in between.

explanation.intuitive: External lines are the particles we prepare and detect. Internal ones are the “message” passed from one vertex to another, which we never see directly.
explanation.scientific: Internal lines represent virtual particles, which propagate between two vertices. They're not on the mass shell, that is, they don't satisfy E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. External lines are real particles that do satisfy it.
explanation.math: Each internal line contributes a propagator. The photon's is −ig_μν/q², where q is the four-momentum it carries.

levels.title: The invisible messenger
levels.intro: Two electrons come in and two electrons go out. Each one touches a vertex, but something is missing between the vertices. Which particle can carry the interaction from one to the other?

steps.prompt: Complete the single virtual photon exchange diagram: choose the right particle and join the two vertices.
hints: Each vertex already has two fermion lines. What's it missing according to the QED rule?
A QED vertex needs exactly one photon: pick the wavy line and join the two vertices.

levels.success: You've built a valid tree-level contribution to electron scattering. Each vertex connects two fermion lines and one photon line.

explanation.intuitive: The two electrons never touch. They “communicate” by exchanging a virtual photon, and that's why they repel each other.
explanation.scientific: It's a tree-level contribution to Møller scattering (e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻) in the t channel. The virtual photon connects two QED vertices and carries the momentum the electrons exchange.
explanation.math: 𝓜_t ∝ [ū(p₃) γ^μ u(p₁)] (1/t) [ū(p₄) γ_μ u(p₂)] · e², with t = (p₁ − p₃)². The smaller the momentum transfer, the larger the contribution: hence the long range of the electric force.

levels.title: Electron versus positron
levels.intro: An electron passes along the top. A positron comes in at the bottom, but its lines aren't drawn yet. Complete the interaction.

steps.prompt: Draw the incoming positron, the outgoing positron and the particle they exchange.
hints: The positron has its arrow against time, both coming in and going out.
From the bottom vertex to the entry; from the exit to the vertex. And a photon between the two vertices.

levels.success: You've drawn Bhabha scattering. Matter and antimatter interacting.

explanation.intuitive: The electron and the positron attract each other (their charges are opposite), and they do it by exchanging a photon, just like two electrons.
explanation.scientific: It's Bhabha scattering in the t channel. The same one-photon exchange describes attraction between opposite charges and repulsion between like charges: the sign is decided by the charge factors and the spinors.
explanation.math: The t-channel contribution is ∝ e²/t. In the non-relativistic limit, this exchange reproduces the Coulomb potential V(r) ∝ ±e²/r.

levels.title: Virtual
levels.intro: Internal lines don't have to be photons. In annihilation, what travels between the two vertices?

steps.prompt: Tap the internal line of the diagram.
steps.wrongDefault: That line touches an edge: it's external.
hints: Look for the line joining the two vertices.
It's straight and vertical.
steps.solved: A straight internal line: a virtual electron.

steps.prompt: That internal line is a virtual electron. What does “virtual” mean?

options.text: It's an internal line: it isn't observed directly and doesn't satisfy the energy–momentum relation of a free particle
options.feedback: Physicists say it's “off the mass shell”.

options.text: That it's imaginary and doesn't affect anything
options.feedback: It matters a lot: without it there'd be no process. Its contribution to the amplitude is real, even if it isn't detected.

options.text: That it travels faster than light
options.feedback: You can't talk about a speed: a diagram doesn't describe trajectories.

hints: Does this line reach any detector?
Think about the difference between internal and external lines.

levels.success: You've understood one of the deepest and most badly explained ideas in physics: virtual particles.

explanation.intuitive: A virtual electron is an electron “in transit”: it only exists as part of the calculation of the interaction and never shows up in a detector.
explanation.scientific: A virtual particle corresponds to a propagator in the amplitude, not to an observable particle. Its four-momentum q doesn't satisfy q² = m²c². That's why it's wrong to picture it as a little ball really travelling between two points.
explanation.math: The electron propagator is i(q̸ + m)/(q² − m²). If the particle were real (q² = m²), the denominator would vanish: the internal line is always off the mass shell.

levels.title: Light from annihilation
levels.intro: An electron and a positron annihilate into two photons. You have the two vertices and the four external particles. Build the complete diagram.

steps.prompt: Join the four external particles to the two vertices and connect the vertices to each other.
hints: Each vertex needs a photon, an arrow coming in and one going out. Put an outgoing photon at each vertex.
Electron to the top vertex, positron to the bottom one (arrow from the vertex toward the entry) and a fermion line between the vertices, from top to bottom.

levels.success: You've built the complete tree-level annihilation, with no lines drawn in advance.

explanation.intuitive: The electron emits a photon, becomes a virtual line and meets the positron, which “absorbs” it by emitting the second photon.
explanation.scientific: It's e⁻e⁺ → γγ annihilation at tree level. The two vertices are joined by a fermion propagator. If you connected the photons the other way round (with the lines crossed), you built the other contribution, which is just as valid.
explanation.math: The total amplitude is 𝓜 = 𝓜_t + 𝓜_u, both ∝ e². Here the relative sign is +, because two identical bosons (the photons) are exchanged.

levels.title: Bouncing light
levels.intro: A photon hits an electron and both come out deflected. It's Compton scattering, the proof that light behaves as a particle.

steps.prompt: Build a Compton scattering diagram: e⁻ γ → e⁻ γ.
hints: No vertex can have two photons. Each external photon goes to a different vertex.
Incoming electron and photon to the left vertex; outgoing electron and photon to the right one; a virtual electron between them.

steps.prompt: In your diagram, which particle travels along the internal line?

options.feedback: The electron absorbs the photon, travels as a virtual line and emits a new photon.
If the internal line were a photon, one vertex would have two photons and the other two electrons with no photon.

hints: Count the photons at each vertex.
Each vertex already has an external photon.

levels.success: You've built Compton scattering, the experiment that confirmed light carries momentum.

explanation.intuitive: The electron “swallows” the photon and spits out another. Light bounces off the electron like a particle.
explanation.scientific: Compton scattering has two tree-level contributions: the s channel (absorption, then emission) and the u channel (emission, then absorption). In both, the internal line is a virtual electron.
explanation.math: The wavelength shift Compton observed in 1923 is Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ). The Klein–Nishina cross-section comes from |𝓜_s + 𝓜_u|².

levels.title: Same diagram, different drawing
levels.intro: We've numbered the particles: 1 and 2 come in, 3 and 4 go out. Are two different drawings two different diagrams? Decide what really matters.

steps.prompt: Do A and B represent the same Feynman diagram?

options.text: Yes: they connect the same particles to the same vertices
options.feedback: The shape of the drawing doesn't matter: only the topology does, that is, what connects to what.

options.text: No: in B the photon is tilted and curved
options.feedback: Geometry has no meaning. Moving vertices or curving lines doesn't change the diagram.

hints: Follow each number to its vertex.
In both, 1 and 3 share a vertex, and so do 2 and 4.

steps.prompt: And these two? Are they the same diagram?

options.text: No: in C electron 1 shares a vertex with exit 4
options.feedback: It changes which final particle is connected to each initial one: it's a different contribution.

options.text: Yes: both have two vertices and a photon
options.feedback: Having the same pieces isn't enough: how they connect matters. In C the lines cross and 1 ends up at 4.

hints: Look at which exit particle 1 shares a vertex with in each drawing.
In A, 1 goes with 3. In C, 1 goes with 4.

levels.success: You've discovered topology: a diagram is a network of connections, not a drawing.

explanation.intuitive: Like on a subway map, you can stretch and bend the lines without changing anything, as long as the connections stay the same.
explanation.scientific: Two diagrams are equivalent if there's a correspondence between their vertices that preserves the connections, the line types and the external particles. Topologically distinct diagrams are different contributions to the amplitude.
explanation.math: The total amplitude is the sum over all topologically distinct diagrams: 𝓜 = Σ 𝓜_i. Counting the same diagram twice would give a wrong result.

levels.title: The other way
levels.intro: Electrons are identical: there's no way to know whether electron 1 ended up at exit 3 or exit 4. Nature takes both possibilities into account.

steps.prompt: Above is the contribution you already know. Build the other tree-level contribution to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻.
hints: In the known one, 1 goes with 3 and 2 goes with 4. Try another pairing.
Join 1 and 4 to one vertex, and 2 and 3 to the other. Then connect the vertices with a photon.

levels.success: You've found the crossed contribution (u channel). For identical particles, both stories count.

explanation.intuitive: If you can't tell the electrons apart, you can't know which went where. Both possibilities contribute at once.
explanation.scientific: Møller scattering has two tree-level diagrams: the t channel (1→3, 2→4) and the u channel (1→4, 2→3). The second exists because the final electrons are indistinguishable.
explanation.math: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_u. The negative relative sign comes from Fermi–Dirac statistics: swapping two identical fermions changes the sign of the amplitude.

levels.title: Bhabha: two stories
levels.intro: An electron and a positron can be deflected by exchanging a photon, as you've seen. But they have another option that two electrons don't.

steps.prompt: Build the annihilation contribution (s channel): electron 1 and positron 2 meet at the same vertex.
hints: The two initial particles go to the left vertex; the final ones, to the right one.
Between the two vertices you need a line that carries no charge.

steps.prompt: In the diagram you've just built, what happens?

options.text: The pair annihilates into a virtual photon, which then creates a new pair
options.feedback: The initial pair disappears completely and a new pair is born from the virtual photon.

options.text: The electron and the positron bounce off without touching
options.feedback: That describes the t channel. Here they meet at the same vertex.

hints: Look at which particles share the left vertex.
After that vertex only a photon remains.

levels.success: You've drawn two different stories for the same process.

explanation.intuitive: Either they're deflected by exchanging a photon, or they turn into a photon and reappear. Both contribute to what we see.
explanation.scientific: Bhabha scattering has two tree-level diagrams: scattering (t channel) and annihilation (s channel). At high energies, the s channel is the basis of e⁺e⁻ colliders such as LEP.
explanation.math: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_s, with propagators 1/t and 1/s, where s = (p₁ + p₂)² is the total centre-of-mass energy squared.

levels.title: Count the contributions
levels.intro: A physicist calculating a process has to find every diagram that contributes, not one more, not one less. Do the count.

steps.prompt: How many tree-level (two-vertex) diagrams contribute to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻?

options.feedback: Remember level 18: identical electrons give one more contribution.
Exactly: the direct one and the crossed one.
The s channel doesn't exist for two electrons. Why? You'll see next.

hints: There are three ways to pair four particles at two vertices.
One of them violates charge conservation.

steps.prompt: Why is there no s-channel diagram for two electrons?

options.text: Two electrons have charge −2, and a photon has none: the arrow couldn't continue at the vertex
options.feedback: Two arrows would come into that vertex and none would leave.
In Bhabha's s channel the electron and the positron do share a vertex. The problem is the charge.

hints: Imagine a vertex with both incoming electrons.
How many arrows come in and how many go out?

steps.prompt: And how many tree-level diagrams contribute to e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺?

options.feedback: In level 19 you built one more.
The u channel would join the initial electron with the final positron at a vertex: the arrows wouldn't flow.
The u channel is impossible here: it would violate charge conservation at the vertex.

hints: Try the three possible pairings.
Initial electron with final positron: is charge conserved?

levels.success: You're doing the first task of a real calculation: finding every diagram.

explanation.intuitive: There are few ways to connect four particles with two vertices, and the rules rule some out. The ones left are all the possible stories.
explanation.scientific: With four external particles there are three pairings (s, t, u). Charge conservation at the vertices removes some. Møller keeps t and u; Bhabha, s and t. This game's engine enumerates these diagrams automatically to check the levels.
explanation.math: At order e², the total amplitude is the sum of the allowed diagrams with their relative signs. The cross-section is ∝ |Σ 𝓜_i|² and includes interference terms between diagrams.

levels.title: Diagnosis
levels.intro: Welcome to the final challenge. There are no more step-by-step instructions. This Compton scattering diagram has two mistakes.

steps.prompt: Fix the diagram so that it's a valid contribution to e⁻γ → e⁻γ. You can flip, delete and redraw the editable lines.
hints: Check the QED rule at each vertex: one photon, one arrow coming in and one going out.
The bottom exit must be a photon, and the internal arrow must go from left to right.

levels.success: Perfect diagnosis. You've repaired a diagram without help.

explanation.intuitive: First you find which rule is broken, then you fix it: that's how you debug any system.
explanation.scientific: The corrected diagram is the s-channel contribution to Compton scattering. The internal arrow continues the flow of the incoming electron, and each vertex has exactly one photon.
explanation.math: 𝓜_s ∝ e² ε*_ν(k′) ū(p′) γ^ν [(p̸ + k̸ + m)/((p + k)² − m²)] γ^μ u(p) ε_μ(k).

levels.title: Light becoming matter
levels.intro: Two photons collide and, from pure light, an electron and a positron are born. Build it without help.

steps.prompt: Build a tree-level diagram for γγ → e⁻e⁺.
hints: Each initial photon goes to a different vertex.
The electron leaves the top vertex, the positron “comes into” the bottom one (arrow toward the vertex) and a virtual electron joins the vertices.

steps.prompt: Your diagram has two vertices. To what power of the charge e is its amplitude 𝓜 proportional?

options.feedback: One factor of e per vertex.
That's the order of the probability, which goes as |𝓜|².

hints: Each vertex contributes a factor e.
Count the vertices.

steps.prompt: The probability of the process is proportional to |𝓜|². What is it proportional to?

options.feedback: With α ≈ 1/137, each extra pair of vertices suppresses the probability about 137 times. That's why perturbation theory works.

hints: Square what you got before.
The fine-structure constant is α = e²/(4πε₀ħc) ≈ 1/137.

levels.success: You've created matter from light and worked out its perturbative order.

explanation.intuitive: The energy of light can turn into matter and antimatter: E = mc² in action.
explanation.scientific: It's the Breit–Wheeler process (γγ → e⁻e⁺), the crossing of annihilation into two photons. It has two tree-level diagrams (t and u channels). It needs photons with enough total energy to create two electron masses.
explanation.math: σ ∝ α² · f(s/m²). Each extra order of perturbation theory (two more vertices, with a loop) contributes a factor α ≈ 1/137.

levels.title: The verdict
levels.intro: Three candidates for contributing to Bhabha scattering (e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺). One of them is an impostor.

steps.prompt: Which one is NOT a valid contribution to e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺?

options.feedback: A is the s channel, annihilation: it's valid.
B is the t channel, scattering: it's valid.
In C, the initial electron and the final positron share a vertex and the arrows don't flow.

hints: Check the arrows at each vertex of each candidate.
Look for a vertex that two arrows arrive at.

steps.prompt: Tap a vertex of the impostor where the QED rule breaks.
steps.wrongDefault: That point is an external particle. Look for the vertices.
hints: In this case, both vertices fail.
Two arrows come into the top one; two go out of the bottom one.
steps.solved: That's where it fails: at a vertex, one arrow must come in and another go out. Charge isn't conserved.

levels.success: You've judged diagrams like a physicist: with the rules, not with visual intuition.

explanation.intuitive: A drawing can look reasonable and be forbidden. The rules never fail.
explanation.scientific: For e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺, the “u” pairing joins the initial e⁻ with the final e⁺. The incoming e⁻ brings charge −1 to the vertex and the outgoing e⁺ takes away +1, so the internal line would have to carry charge −2. A photon is neutral, so that diagram doesn't exist. Visually, two arrows come into the same vertex.
explanation.math: Current conservation at each vertex cancels any term of this kind in the perturbative expansion: only 𝓜_s and 𝓜_t contribute.

levels.title: Grand finale: complete Møller
levels.intro: A particle physics student's final exam: write down every tree-level diagram for electron–electron scattering and say how they combine.

steps.prompt: Build the t-channel contribution: 1 → 3 and 2 → 4.
hints: 1 and 3 share a vertex; 2 and 4, the other.
A photon between the vertices.

steps.prompt: Now the crossed contribution, the u channel: 1 → 4 and 2 → 3.
hints: The lines will have to cross.
1 and 4 to the top vertex; 2 and 3 to the bottom one.

steps.prompt: To get the total amplitude you have to combine the two diagrams. Since electrons are identical fermions, how do they combine?

options.text: Their amplitudes are subtracted: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_u
options.feedback: Swapping two identical fermions changes the sign of the amplitude (Pauli exclusion principle).
In quantum mechanics amplitudes are added, not probabilities, and that's why interference appears.
Both are equally simple (two vertices) and contribute at the same order e².

hints: In quantum mechanics, amplitudes are added, not probabilities.
Fermions are antisymmetric under exchange.

levels.success: You've mastered tree level: you read, build and judge Feynman diagrams. Now the real thing begins: more vertices and quantum loops.

explanation.intuitive: Two indistinguishable stories produce the same final result, and nature combines them with a minus sign that comes from the very nature of electrons.
explanation.scientific: The tree-level Møller amplitude is the difference of the t and u channels. The interference between them is a measurable prediction, confirmed by experiment, and a direct consequence of the Pauli principle.
explanation.math: 𝓜 = e² { [ū₃γ^μu₁][ū₄γ_μu₂]/t − [ū₄γ^μu₁][ū₃γ_μu₂]/u }, with t = (p₁ − p₃)² and u = (p₁ − p₄)².

levels.title: A bonus photon
levels.intro: When two electrons collide, sometimes an extra photon flies out: braking radiation. Two vertices are no longer enough.

steps.prompt: Build e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ using all three vertices: the electrons exchange a photon and the top one then emits a real photon.
hints: Follow electron 1's line: it comes in, interacts, emits and goes out. Each stop is a vertex.
Top: 1 → left vertex → right vertex → 3. The right vertex emits the real photon; the left one exchanges a photon with electron 2.

steps.prompt: This process has one more vertex than Møller scattering. How does its probability change?

options.feedback: Each vertex adds a factor e to the amplitude: it can't be the same.

options.text: It's about 137 times less likely (a factor α)
options.feedback: The amplitude gains a factor e; the probability, e², that is, α ≈ 1/137.

options.text: It's more likely, because there are more particles
options.feedback: More vertices means more factors of e, and e is small.

hints: Amplitude ∝ eⁿ, with n the number of vertices.
The probability is |𝓜|²: each extra vertex multiplies it by e², which is proportional to α.

levels.success: You've built your first three-vertex diagram: a process with radiation.

explanation.intuitive: A charge that suddenly changes direction emits light. Here, the light comes out of the electron that has just been pushed.
explanation.scientific: It's braking radiation (bremsstrahlung) in Møller scattering. It's a process of order e³ in the amplitude: it's suppressed by a factor α compared with scattering without a photon, but it dominates the energy loss of fast electrons in matter.
explanation.math: 𝓜 ∝ e³. dσ(ee → eeγ) ∼ α · dσ(ee → ee) · (emission factor), with dσ ∝ α³ overall.

levels.title: How many stories?
levels.intro: With three vertices, the extra photon can come out of many places. Before calculating, a physicist counts all the possible stories.

steps.prompt: Play the diagram in time. When is the real photon emitted?

options.feedback: Look at the order of the vertices: the real photon comes out of the last one.

options.text: There's no real photon, only the virtual one
options.feedback: The wavy line ending at the right edge is a real outgoing photon.

hints: Press ▶ and watch which vertex lights up last.
The right vertex, which emits the real photon, is the last one in time.

steps.prompt: In this other story, tap the vertex where the real photon is born.

wrong.vA: That vertex emits the virtual photon the electrons exchange.
wrong.vB: That vertex absorbs the virtual photon.

steps.wrongDefault: Look for a vertex: the points on the edges are external particles.
hints: Follow the wavy line that ends at the edge.
It's on electron 2's line, before the exchange.
steps.solved: Here electron 2 radiates before interacting. It's another contribution to the same process.

steps.prompt: The real photon can come out of any of the 4 electron lines, and there are 2 ways to pair up the electrons (t and u). How many tree-level diagrams does e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ have?

options.feedback: That only counts one pairing. Remember the t and u channels.
4 lines to attach the photon to × 2 channels = 8 stories.
The photon can't come out of the virtual line: a photon has no charge and doesn't emit another photon.

hints: Multiply the independent possibilities.
4 external electron lines × 2 pairings.

levels.success: Counting the stories correctly is the first step of any real calculation.

explanation.intuitive: Each place where the photon can be born is a different story. Nature goes through all of them at once.
explanation.scientific: There are 8 tree-level diagrams for e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻γ: the photon attaches to any of the 4 external electron lines, in the t and u channels. The 8 amplitudes are added (with Pauli's relative sign between t and u) before squaring.
explanation.math: 𝓜 = Σᵢ 𝓜ᵢ, with 8 terms ∝ e³. The game checks this by enumerating every trivalent tree with 5 leaves that satisfies the vertex rule.

levels.title: Three flashes
levels.intro: Positronium is a short-lived atom: an electron and a positron orbiting each other. One of its forms dies by emitting three photons.

steps.prompt: Build e⁻e⁺ → γγγ. A single fermion line runs through all three vertices and each vertex emits a photon.
hints: The arrow comes in with the electron, passes through all three vertices and goes out toward the positron.
Electron → top vertex → middle vertex → bottom vertex → positron (arrow toward the positron). One photon at each vertex.

steps.prompt: The three photons are identical. How many different diagrams are there, changing which photon comes out of each vertex?

options.feedback: Try swapping two photons: it connects the same particles differently.
3 · 2 · 1 = 6 ways to share three photons among three vertices.

hints: The first vertex can emit any of the 3 photons; the second, either of the 2 left.

levels.success: You've drawn the decay of ortho-positronium.

explanation.intuitive: Matter and antimatter meet and turn into three flashes of light.
explanation.scientific: Positronium with parallel spins (ortho-positronium) can't decay into two photons: charge-conjugation symmetry forbids it. That's why it emits three, lives about a thousand times longer than para-positronium (which emits two), and its decay rate is a precision test of QED.
explanation.math: 6 diagrams, each ∝ e³. Γ(o-Ps → 3γ) ∝ α⁶ mₑ, versus Γ(p-Ps → 2γ) ∝ α⁵ mₑ.

levels.title: Permutations
levels.intro: Identical photons don't have names of their own. Swapping them gives another story that also counts.

steps.prompt: Build a contribution to e⁻e⁺ → γγγ different from the reference one.
hints: The electron line is already there. You only have to decide which photon comes out of each vertex.
Swap two photons compared with the reference: for example, 1 from the middle vertex and 2 from the top one.

steps.prompt: In Møller, the two diagrams were subtracted. How do these six contributions with identical photons combine?

options.text: They all add with the same sign
options.feedback: Photons are bosons: swapping them doesn't change the sign of the amplitude.

options.text: The signs alternate, as in Møller
options.feedback: The minus sign appears when swapping identical fermions, not bosons.

options.text: Only one counts, because the photons are the same
options.feedback: Precisely because they're indistinguishable, every story contributes.

hints: Are photons fermions or bosons?
Pauli's minus sign only appears with identical fermions.

levels.success: You can now tell how identical bosons and fermions combine.

explanation.intuitive: Swapping two identical photons gives a new story, just as valid, that adds to the others.
explanation.scientific: For identical bosons the amplitude is symmetric under exchange: the 6 permutations add with a + sign. For identical fermions it's antisymmetric (Møller's − sign). This difference explains Bose–Einstein statistics and the Pauli exclusion principle.
explanation.math: 𝓜 = Σ_{σ ∈ S₃} 𝓜(k_σ(1), k_σ(2), k_σ(3)), with a + sign for every term.

levels.title: A closed circuit
levels.intro: Until now everything was a tree. But nature also allows stories that loop back on themselves: loops.

steps.prompt: This diagram has a loop. Select all the lines that form the closed circuit.
steps.wrongDefault: That line isn't part of the circuit. Look for a path that leaves a vertex and comes back to it.
hints: Start from the top-left vertex and look for a path back to it without repeating lines.
The loop is made of the curved photon at the top and the two electron segments below it.
steps.solved: That's the loop: a photon emitted and reabsorbed by the same electron.

steps.prompt: In a tree, momentum conservation fixes the momentum of each internal line. What happens with the lines of a loop?

options.feedback: In a closed circuit momentum can “go round” without the external particles noticing.

options.text: It can have any value and you have to add them all up
options.feedback: Each loop adds an integral over a free momentum.
Nothing forces it to be zero: any value is compatible with conservation.

hints: Imagine an amount of momentum entering the loop and going all the way round.
The external particles can't know how much momentum circulates inside.

steps.prompt: This diagram has 4 vertices. How much smaller is its amplitude than that of the Møller tree?

options.text: A factor e², that is, ∝ α
options.feedback: Two more vertices: e⁴ versus e². That's why loops are small corrections.
Count the vertices: 4 versus 2.

hints: Amplitude ∝ eⁿ, with n the number of vertices.
e⁴ / e² = e².

levels.success: You can now recognise a loop and you know why it's a small correction.

explanation.intuitive: In a loop, the virtual particle can carry any amount of momentum. Nature tries them all.
explanation.scientific: Each independent loop leaves a momentum that isn't fixed by conservation at the vertices; you have to integrate over it. These integrals can diverge, and renormalization is the technique that tames them. Each loop adds two vertices: a factor α in the relative amplitude.
explanation.math: 𝓜₁ ∝ e⁴ ∫ d⁴ℓ/(2π)⁴ [propagators with ℓ]. Loops: L = I − V + 1, with I internal lines and V vertices.

levels.title: The vacuum boils
levels.intro: The photon exchanged by two electrons can turn, for an instant, into an electron–positron pair and become a photon again.

steps.prompt: Complete the loop between the two central vertices: the virtual photon turns into an e⁻e⁺ pair that annihilates again.
hints: Each central vertex already has its photon. It's missing the two fermion lines.
Draw two fermion lines between the two central vertices, with arrows in opposite directions. The second one curves by itself.

steps.prompt: These virtual pairs surround each electron like a cloud that screens its charge. What happens when you get very close to the electron (at high energies)?

options.text: You get through the cloud and the effective charge increases
options.feedback: α grows with energy: from ≈ 1/137 to ≈ 1/128 at the energy of the Z boson.
The opposite happens: the cloud screens, so inside it you see more charge.

options.text: The charge is always the same
options.feedback: The “bare” charge doesn't change, but the one we measure depends on the distance.

hints: Think of the cloud of pairs as a dielectric surrounding the charge.
Inside the cloud there's less screening.

levels.success: You've drawn vacuum polarization: the quantum vacuum isn't empty.

explanation.intuitive: Empty space is full of particle–antiparticle pairs that appear and disappear. They surround each charge and screen it.
explanation.scientific: Vacuum polarization makes the coupling constant depend on energy: α(0) ≈ 1/137, but α(m_Z) ≈ 1/128. It was the first “constant” seen to change, and the contribution can be measured in the Lamb shift of hydrogen.
explanation.math: Π(q²) ≈ (α/3π) ln(−q²/m²) for |q²| ≫ m²; α_eff(q²) = α / (1 − Π(q²)).

levels.title: Schwinger's number
levels.intro: An electron crosses a magnetic field. In 1948, Julian Schwinger calculated how a loop changes its internal magnet. The result is engraved on his tombstone.

steps.prompt: Build the vertex correction: the electron emits a virtual photon, interacts with the field and reabsorbs the photon.
hints: The electron line passes through all three vertices: left, middle and right.
Electron → left → middle → right → exit, and a photon joins the left vertex to the right one.

steps.prompt: Without the loop, the electron's “g-factor” is exactly 2. The loop corrects it: a = (g − 2)/2. What is that correction?

options.feedback: It's a one-loop correction: it must be of order α.
Schwinger's result. Today it's known up to five loops and agrees with experiment to more than 10 digits.
If it were zero, the loop would have no effect. It does, and it's measured.

hints: A loop contributes a factor α compared with the tree.
α ≈ 1/137, and it appears divided by 2π.

levels.success: You've drawn one of the most famous diagrams in physics.

explanation.intuitive: The electron isn't alone: it carries a cloud of virtual photons that slightly changes how it responds to a magnet.
explanation.scientific: The electron's anomalous magnetic moment, a = α/2π at one loop, is the most precise prediction in physics: theory and experiment agree to more than 10 significant figures. With this arrangement of vertices another one-loop correction is also valid: the self-energy of an external line.
explanation.math: Γ^μ = γ^μ F₁(q²) + (iσ^{μν}q_ν / 2m) F₂(q²), with a = F₂(0) = α/2π + 𝒪(α²).

levels.title: Light on light
levels.intro: Two beams of light cross without touching... almost always. Can a photon bounce off another?

steps.prompt: Is there any tree-level diagram (without loops) for γγ → γγ?

options.text: Yes, joining the four photons at two vertices
options.feedback: Each QED vertex needs two fermion lines. Here no fermion comes in or goes out.

options.text: No: with no external fermions, the fermion lines have to close into a loop

hints: Count how many fermion lines each vertex needs.
A fermion line can only end at an edge or carry on. If there are no fermions at the edges...

steps.prompt: Build the box diagram: join the four vertices with fermion lines.
hints: Each vertex already has its photon. It's missing an arrow coming in and one going out.
Go round the square in a single direction: top-left → top-right → bottom-right → bottom-left → back to the start.

levels.success: Light can scatter light, but only through a loop of virtual matter.

explanation.intuitive: Photons don't interact directly: they need the vacuum to lend them, for an instant, an electron and a positron.
explanation.scientific: Light-by-light scattering doesn't exist in classical physics and in QED it first appears at one loop. There are 6 box diagrams. ATLAS observed it in 2017 in collisions of lead ions, whose huge electric fields act as photon beams.
explanation.math: 𝓜(γγ → γγ) ∝ e⁴, σ ∝ α⁴. At low energy, the effect is described by the Euler–Heisenberg Lagrangian.

levels.title: Furry's theorem
levels.intro: Some diagrams follow every rule and, even so, their total contribution is exactly zero.

steps.prompt: Which of these loops does NOT contribute to any process?

options.feedback: The four-photon box exists: it's light-by-light scattering.
This bubble is vacuum polarization: it has measurable effects.
An electron loop with an odd number of photons cancels out.

hints: Count how many photons attach to each electron loop.
Look for the loop with an odd number of photons.

steps.prompt: The triangle can be traversed in both directions. Both diagrams are valid. What happens when you add them?

options.text: They add up: the effect doubles
options.feedback: Reversing the loop is the same as swapping electron for positron, and each photon changes sign under that operation.
With 3 photons, reversing the loop gives a sign (−1)³ = −1.
The cancellation is exact, for any photon momenta.

hints: Reversing the arrows is the same as swapping electrons for positrons.
Each photon contributes a sign −1 under that operation.

levels.success: You've spotted a valid diagram that contributes nothing: a symmetry cancels it.

explanation.intuitive: Two identical stories, but traversed in opposite directions, balance each other perfectly.
explanation.scientific: Furry's theorem (1937) says that a closed electron loop with an odd number of photons doesn't contribute. It's a consequence of charge-conjugation symmetry: the photon is odd under C. The game's validator applies it: if you build a loop like that, it will warn you.
explanation.math: C A_μ C⁻¹ = −A_μ ⇒ ⟨0|T{A_μ₁ ⋯ A_μₙ}|0⟩ = 0 for odd n. The two orientations add to 𝓜 + (−1)ⁿ𝓜.

levels.title: Grand finale: Møller at one loop
levels.intro: A PhD student's exam: go beyond the tree in electron–electron scattering.

steps.prompt: Build a one-loop correction to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻ using all four vertices. Try the box diagram: the electrons exchange two photons.
hints: Each electron passes through two vertices: the top one through the top two, the bottom one through the bottom two.
1 → top-left → top-right → 3; 2 → bottom-left → bottom-right → 4; and two vertical photons between the two lines.

steps.prompt: The probability is |𝓜_tree + 𝓜_loop|². The loop's first effect is the cross term 2·Re(𝓜_tree* · 𝓜_loop). At what order does it contribute?

options.feedback: The tree alone already gives α². The cross term has more vertices.

options.text: α³: an order-α correction to the tree result
options.feedback: e² · e⁴ = e⁶ ∝ α³. That's why the tree is enough for ~1% precision.
That's |𝓜_loop|², which is even smaller.

hints: 𝓜_tree ∝ e², 𝓜_loop ∝ e⁴.
Multiply: e² · e⁴, and remember that α ∝ e².

levels.success: Campaign complete. You've gone from the quantum alphabet to one-loop corrections.

explanation.intuitive: Each level of detail adds more complicated stories, and each one weighs about a hundred times less than the one before. That's how QED can make such astonishingly precise predictions.
explanation.scientific: At one loop, Møller scattering gets vertex, vacuum polarization, self-energy and box (direct and crossed) corrections. They're all ∝ α relative to the tree, and some have infrared divergences that only cancel when you add the braking radiation from chapter 6.
explanation.math: σ = σ₀ [1 + (α/π) C + 𝒪(α²)], with σ₀ ∝ α². The infrared divergences cancel between ee → ee (one loop) and ee → eeγ (Bloch–Nordsieck theorem).

concepts.title: Electron
concepts.summary: A straight line with the arrow pointing forward in time.
concepts.body: An elementary particle with charge −1, responsible for chemistry and electricity. It is a fermion: two identical electrons cannot occupy the same state.

concepts.title: Photon
concepts.summary: A wavy line. The particle of light.
concepts.body: The quantum of the electromagnetic field. It has no mass and no charge. It carries the electromagnetic force between charged particles.

concepts.title: Time convention
concepts.summary: Time runs from left to right.
concepts.body: On the left we draw the initial state (what comes in) and on the right the final state (what goes out). Other books use the vertical axis: it's just a convention.

concepts.title: Initial and final state
concepts.summary: What comes in and what goes out.
concepts.body: External lines represent the real particles that are prepared and detected. Everything else happens in between.

concepts.title: Positron
concepts.summary: A straight line with the arrow pointing backward in time.
concepts.body: The electron's antiparticle: same mass and charge +1. Dirac predicted it in 1928 and Anderson discovered it in 1932.

concepts.title: Annihilation
concepts.summary: Matter and antimatter turn into light.
concepts.body: An electron and a positron disappear and produce two photons. It's the principle behind PET scans in medicine.

concepts.title: Not a trajectory
concepts.summary: A diagram is a piece of a calculation, not a photo.
concepts.body: Feynman diagrams represent contributions to a probability amplitude. The positions and angles in the drawing have no physical meaning.

concepts.title: QED vertex
concepts.summary: Three lines: an arrow in, an arrow out and a photon.
concepts.body: The only fundamental interaction of quantum electrodynamics. Each vertex contributes a factor of the charge e.

concepts.title: Charge conservation
concepts.summary: Arrows never break.
concepts.body: At every vertex, one arrow comes in and another goes out. The total charge before and after any process is the same.

concepts.title: Forbidden vertices
concepts.summary: No four lines and no two photons at a vertex.
concepts.body: QED has only one fundamental vertex. More complex processes are built by chaining three-line vertices.

concepts.title: Allowed ≠ possible
concepts.summary: A correct vertex is not a possible process on its own.
concepts.body: Processes with three real free particles violate conservation of energy and momentum. A vertex is a piece of a bigger diagram.

concepts.title: Crossing symmetry
concepts.summary: A rotated vertex tells another story.
concepts.body: Emission, absorption, annihilation and pair creation are the same vertex oriented in different ways with respect to time.

concepts.title: Internal and external lines
concepts.summary: External: observable. Internal: virtual.
concepts.body: An external line touches an edge of the diagram. An internal one joins two vertices and represents a virtual particle.

concepts.title: Møller scattering
concepts.summary: Two electrons repel each other by exchanging a photon.
concepts.body: It has two tree-level diagrams, t and u, which are subtracted because electrons are identical fermions.

concepts.title: Virtual photon
concepts.summary: The force's invisible messenger.
concepts.body: An internal photon that carries momentum between two vertices. It never reaches a detector and doesn't satisfy the energy–momentum relation of a free photon.

concepts.title: Bhabha scattering
concepts.summary: Electron versus positron.
concepts.body: It has two contributions: scattering (t channel) and annihilation (s channel). It's used to measure the luminosity of colliders.

concepts.title: Virtual electron
concepts.summary: An internal fermion line.
concepts.body: It appears in annihilation and in Compton scattering. Its propagator is i(q̸ + m)/(q² − m²).

concepts.title: Tree level
concepts.summary: Diagrams without loops.
concepts.body: They are the simplest (lowest-order) contributions to a process. Loops are smaller corrections, suppressed by factors of α ≈ 1/137.

concepts.title: Compton scattering
concepts.summary: Light bounces off an electron.
concepts.body: Its discovery in 1923 showed that light carries momentum like a particle. It has contributions from the s and u channels.

concepts.title: Topology
concepts.summary: What matters is what connects to what, not how it's drawn.
concepts.body: Two drawings with the same connections are the same diagram. Topologically different diagrams are different contributions.

concepts.title: Identical particles
concepts.summary: If you can't tell them apart, every story counts.
concepts.body: With two identical final electrons you must include both the direct and the crossed diagram.

concepts.title: s, t and u channels
concepts.summary: The three ways to pair up four particles.
concepts.body: s: the two initial particles share a vertex. t: each initial particle with “its” final one. u: crossed. The charge rules decide which ones exist.

concepts.title: Counting diagrams
concepts.summary: Every diagram, not one more, not one less.
concepts.body: The first step of a calculation is to list every topologically distinct contribution at the desired order.

concepts.title: Pair production
concepts.summary: Matter from light.
concepts.body: Two photons with enough energy can create an electron and a positron (the Breit–Wheeler process).

concepts.title: Perturbative order
concepts.summary: Each vertex contributes a factor e.
concepts.body: With n vertices, the amplitude goes as eⁿ. Since α ≈ 1/137 is small, diagrams with more vertices contribute less and less.

concepts.title: Bremsstrahlung
concepts.summary: A deflected charge emits light.
concepts.body: German for “braking radiation”. It's a three-vertex process, suppressed by a factor of α compared with scattering without a photon. It's how fast electrons lose energy in matter and how X-ray tubes work.

concepts.title: Positronium
concepts.summary: An atom of matter and antimatter.
concepts.body: A bound electron and positron. With parallel spins (ortho-positronium) it can only decay into three photons and lives about 142 ns; with opposite spins (para-positronium), into two, and it lives about 0.12 ns.

concepts.title: Identical bosons
concepts.summary: Swapping them doesn't change the sign.
concepts.body: The amplitudes of identical photons add with the same sign (symmetric). Those of identical fermions, with alternating sign (antisymmetric). That's where lasers and the exclusion principle come from.

concepts.title: Loop
concepts.summary: A closed circuit of internal lines.
concepts.body: Each loop leaves a free momentum that has to be integrated over. Loops are quantum corrections suppressed by a factor of α, and studying them led to renormalization.

concepts.title: Vacuum polarization
concepts.summary: The vacuum screens charges.
concepts.body: Virtual electron–positron pairs make the effective charge grow at short distances: α goes from ≈ 1/137 to ≈ 1/128 at the energy of the Z boson.

concepts.title: Anomalous magnetic moment
concepts.summary: a = α/2π: Schwinger's result.
concepts.body: The vertex loop corrects the electron's magnet by 0.116%. It's the most precise prediction in science: theory and experiment agree to more than 10 digits.

concepts.title: Light on light
concepts.summary: Photons bouncing off each other.
concepts.body: Impossible in classical physics. In QED it happens through a loop of virtual electrons (6 box diagrams). ATLAS observed it in 2017.

concepts.title: Furry's theorem
concepts.summary: Loops with an odd number of photons cancel out.
concepts.body: The two orientations of an electron loop cancel when it carries an odd number of photons. It's a consequence of charge-conjugation symmetry.

concepts.title: Interference
concepts.summary: Amplitudes add, not probabilities.
concepts.body: Diagrams are combined before squaring. For identical fermions, the exchange contributes a minus sign.

identify.prompt: What process does this diagram represent?
identify.feedback: First read the particles on the left (coming in), then the ones on the right (going out).
hints: Identify the particles coming in on the left.
Arrow forward in time: e⁻. Against time: e⁺. Wavy: γ.

internal.prompt: Tap the internal line (the virtual particle).
internal.wrongDefault: That line touches an edge: it's external.
hints: Look for the line joining two vertices.
It doesn't touch any edge of the diagram.

species.wrongDefault: Look at the kind of line, its arrow and which side it's on.
species.hintIn: What comes in is on the left.
species.hintOut: What goes out is on the right.
species.hint: Arrow forward in time: e⁻. Against time: e⁺. Wavy: γ.

validity.prompt: Does this diagram follow the rules of QED?
validity.valid: Each vertex has a photon, an arrow coming in and another going out.
hints: Check the vertices one by one.
At each vertex: exactly one photon, one arrow coming in and one going out.

channel.prompt: What kind of contribution (channel) is this diagram?

options.s: s channel: the two initial particles share a vertex
options.t: t channel: each initial particle shares a vertex with the final one on the same side

channel.feedback: Look at which particles share the vertex with the top-left one.
hints: Look at the top-left particle.
Does it share a vertex with the other initial particle (s), with the top final one (t) or with the bottom final one (u)?
